passages.original: qua] et regio circumposita Babylonia vo- catur. Hanc fuisse potentissimam1, et in campe- stribus per quadrum sitam, ab angulo usque ad angulum muri, sedecim millia passuum tenuisse, id est, simul per circuitum sexaginta quatuor millia, refert Herodotus et mulli alii, qui Graecas histo- rias conscripserunt. Arx autem, id est, Capitolium illius urbis, est turris, quae post diluvium aedificata (Gen.XI, 5), quatuor millia passuum tenere dici- tur : cujus post ruinam, muri tantum fictiles re- mansisse, et ob bestias, quae illic abundant ca- ptandas, recuperati esse traduntur.
passages.english: [from which] the surrounding region is also called Babylonia. Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that it was very powerful, and that it was laid out as a square on the plains, and that its wall extended sixteen thousand paces from corner to corner, that is, sixty-four thousand in all around its circuit. The citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is the tower which was built after the Flood (Gen. 11:5), and it is said to extend four thousand paces; after its ruin, it is reported, only the walls of baked clay remained, and they were restored for the purpose of catching the wild beasts which abound there.
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-sentence after an editorial bracket ('[Al.' in the preceding context, an alternative reading); 'qua]' closes it, here rendered 'from which'. 'mulli' read as 'multi'. The footnote mark '1' after 'potentissimam' is omitted.

passages.original: Smyrna, civitas Lyciae provinciae in Asia : cujus Lucas ita meminit : Et pelagus Ciliciae et Pamphy- liae navigantes venimus in Smyrnam6 Lyciae (Act.XXVII, 5). Pro quo aliqui codices habent : Venimus in Lystram, quae est in Cilicia. Porro Hieronymus in libris Hebraeorum nominum ponit Smyrnam, et interpretatur, amaram.
passages.english: Smyrna, a city of the province of Lycia in Asia. Luke mentions it thus: "And sailing across the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia we came to Smyrna of Lycia" (Acts 27:5). In place of this some manuscripts have: "We came to Lystra, which is in Cilicia." Further, Jerome in his books of Hebrew names lists Smyrna and interprets it as 'bitter'.
passages.notes: The footnote mark '6' after 'Smyrnam' is omitted. The usual text of Acts 27:5 reads Myra of Lycia; the author's 'Smyrna' and the variant 'Lystra' are translated as given.
